# Jeremiah 45 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This is the shortest chapter in the Book of Jeremiah (5 verses), a personal oracle addressed to Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah’s scribe. Chronologically it belongs after Jeremiah 36 (the fourth year of Jehoiakim, c. 605 BC), though placed here at the end of Jeremiah’s prophecies to Judah. It is a window into the inner life of a discouraged servant of God and God’s pointed but merciful response.

---

## v. 1 — The Historical Setting

> *“This is the word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch son of Neriah when he wrote these words on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Baruch as Jeremiah’s amanuensis.** Baruch was Jeremiah’s trusted scribe who wrote down the prophet’s words at his dictation. Later both were taken to Egypt against their will (Jeremiah 43:6). He is the only man from the Old Testament who has been “fingerprinted” — in 1975, archaeologists discovered a clay document marker (bulla) bearing his seal and a thumbprint, very probably his own. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)

- **A misplaced chapter chronologically.** The events belong after Jeremiah 36:8 or 36:32, when Baruch wrote the scroll that King Jehoiakim burned. Gill notes this was “eighteen years before the destruction of Jerusalem” and the prophecy is postponed to this place because it was written to a private person. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/45.htm)

- **Ellicott** concurs: “The chapter is obviously misplaced as far as chronological order is concerned, and ought to follow on Jeremiah 35, 36.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-45.html)

- **Constable** adds that perhaps the editor placed it here “to show that Yahweh exempted faithful Baruch from the threats to the Judean remnant recorded in chapter 44,” and that it is “the last chapter in the book in which Jeremiah is part of the narrative.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-45.html)

- **Baruch arranged it here himself.** According to Ryken (cited by Guzik), “when Baruch arranged Jeremiah’s scroll he put this prophecy right where it belonged. He treasured the promise God gave him… So he put it here at the end of his life to show that God was faithful to his promise.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)

---

## vv. 2–3 — Baruch’s Complaint

> *“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says to you, Baruch: You have said, ‘Woe is me because the LORD has added sorrow to my pain! I am worn out with groaning and have found no rest.’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- **God knows Baruch by name.** Gill notes God “knew him by name, had a great regard for him,” and addresses him as “the God of Israel” to remind him of the covenant relationship. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/45.htm)

- **God hears unspoken complaints.** Baruch may have spoken this inwardly. God heard and responded — a sobering reality that God knows our private thoughts.

- **The source of Baruch’s distress.** Several reasons converge:
  - The dangerous nature of his work: copying prophecies of doom, reading them publicly, and the king’s order to arrest both Jeremiah and Baruch (Jeremiah 36:26). Adam Clarke notes, “He had mourned for the desolations that were coming on his country, and now he mourns for the dangers to which he feels his own life exposed.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)
  - The content of what he was transcribing: prophecies of national ruin would naturally depress someone who loved his people.
  - Gill adds the king’s burning of the scroll, then requiring Baruch to rewrite it with added threats, compounded his grief. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/45.htm)

- **Self-centredness in the complaint.** Cundall (cited by Guzik) observes “the self-centeredness of his attitude indicated by the five personal pronouns in verse 3 (the same number in the Pharisee’s self-congratulatory prayer, Luke 18:11f.).” G. Campbell Morgan adds: “The emphasis in his lamentation is to be placed on the word ‘me’ – ‘Woe is me now.’” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)

- **Physical and spiritual exhaustion.** Constable notes that “Baruch had complained about the sorrow, pain, inner turmoil, and restlessness that he had experienced because he carried out God’s will. His lament recalls Jeremiah’s ‘confessions’ and some of the personal lament psalms.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-45.html)

- **Jewish tradition** (Jarchi, Kimchi, and others, cited by Gill) interpreted Baruch’s grief as disappointment over not receiving the gift of prophecy himself. Baruch is represented as comparing himself to Joshua (who succeeded Moses) and Elisha (who succeeded Elijah), asking why the prophetic spirit had not come upon him. Gill calls this “a foolish conceit.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/45.htm)

**Reformed / Baptist (DesiringGod – Piper):** Greg Morse, writing for Desiring God, identifies deeply with Baruch’s complaint, noting: “Sometimes — not all the time, but sometimes — our fatigue as men comes less from our great self-sacrifices and more from our selfish ambition.” He notes that Baruch “expected praise and received persecution. And this disappointment added bitterness to his sorrow, weariness to his pain. The weeds of frustrated vanity slowly choked his manly fortitude.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/secret-pride-makes-a-man-fragile)

---

## v. 4 — God’s Perspective: A Bigger Picture

> *“Thus Jeremiah was to say to Baruch: ‘This is what the LORD says: Throughout the land I will demolish what I have built and uproot what I have planted.’”*

**Traditional Reading:**

- **God’s own sorrow.** Before addressing Baruch’s complaint, God puts things in perspective: He Himself is about to destroy what He built and uproot what He planted. Thompson (cited by Guzik) says: “Jeremiah had to remind Baruch of God’s own sorrow at what was to happen… Yahweh had built something and was about to destroy it.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)

- **Echoes Jeremiah’s original commission.** The language of “build…break down…plant…pluck up” echoes Jeremiah 1:10, the prophet’s original call. Constable notes this connection to Jeremiah 1:10; 2:21; 31:5. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-45.html)

- **The whole land.** Gill emphasises “not a few cities only, or only Jerusalem the metropolis, but the whole land of Judea; no part of it but what should be left desolate.” This is judgment on “the Jewish nation, both as to church and state.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/45.htm)

- **A word for Baruch personally.** Guzik notes: “Baruch was used to writing out what God spoke to Jeremiah for others, not for himself. God had a word for His discouraged, exhausted servant.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)

**Reformed view (Monergism / Thomas Manton):** Manton, the Puritan, saw God’s speech in v. 4 as a rebuke to Baruch’s self-preoccupation: “Are thy concerns more precious than the temple or salvation of my people? Leave off this dream of a pleasant life in this world.” The “great things” Baruch sought were “a prosperous and peaceable estate for his own particular, or quiet, ease, and safety in the midst of so great calamity.” (https://www.monergism.com/do-you-seek-great-things-yourself-seek-them-not-jeremiah-455)

---

## v. 5 — The Rebuke and the Promise

> *“But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking! For I will bring disaster on every living creature, declares the LORD, but wherever you go, I will grant your life as a spoil of war.”*

**Traditional Reading:**

### “Do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking!”

- **The heart of Baruch’s problem.** Most commentators agree that Baruch’s despondency was partly rooted in disappointed ambition. Ellicott describes him as having “an ambitious temperament eager to take the lead… He had, it may be, drawn for himself an ideal picture of a successful work, in which he himself should be a chief agent.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-45.html)

- **What were the “great things”?** Several suggestions:
  - **Gill:** “Riches and wealth, honour and esteem, peace and prosperity.” Baruch may have hoped his service in reading the scroll to the princes would lead to “preferring him at court, of advancing him to some post or office.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/45.htm)
  - **Feinberg:** “He may have had hopes of attaining a high office or even of receiving the gift of prophecy.” (Cited by Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)
  - **Constable:** Baruch came from a distinguished family — his brother was a high official under Zedekiah (Jeremiah 51:59) and his grandfather had been ruler of Jerusalem under Josiah (2 Chronicles 34:8). He “may have entertained hopes of attaining a position of distinction in the nation.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-45.html)
  - **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** “The seeking of greatness for one’s self lies at the very root of man’s problem.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-45.html)

- **Not a ban on all ambition.** Constable clarifies: “The Lord’s command not to seek great things for himself presupposes a proud motive. Seeking to serve the Lord in a significant position of ministry is not wrong in itself, provided one’s motive is to glorify God.” Guzik likewise notes that Paul, Peter, and even Jesus were ambitious — “ambitious for God’s glory and fame.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)

### “I will bring disaster on every living creature”

- **Scope of judgment.** Gill clarifies “all flesh” refers to “all the inhabitants of Judea, who should either die by the sword or by famine, or by pestilence, or be carried captive.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/45.htm) Barnes extends it further: “It was not Judaea only but the whole known world that was thrown into turmoil by Nebuchadnezzar’s energy (Jeremiah 25:26).” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/45-5.htm)

- **Perspective.** The nearness of universal judgment makes the pursuit of personal greatness absurd.

### “Your life as a spoil of war”

- **Military imagery.** Thompson notes, “The figure is of a soldier barely escaping with his life after a defeat in battle.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/) It is not a promise of prosperity or honour — just survival. JFB Commentary: “Esteem it enough at such a general crisis that thy life shall be granted thee.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/45-5.htm)

- **A distinguishing mercy.** Gill: “He should be snatched as a brand out of the burning… he should lose everything, yet not his life; which should be as dear to him as a rich spoil taken by the soldier, being a distinguishing mercy.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/45.htm)

- **Fulfilled.** Baruch survived the fall of Jerusalem, was taken to Egypt (Jeremiah 43:6), and tradition says he may have gone to Babylon (Baruch 1:1). The promise held wherever he went.

---

## The Spurgeon Connection (v. 5)

Charles Spurgeon testified that as a young man of eighteen, after missing an interview at Regent’s Park College, he was bitterly disappointed. As he walked through the countryside, Jeremiah 45:5 came to mind: “Seekest thou great things for thyself? Seek them not!” He never attended college, yet became perhaps the most famous preacher in Victorian England. (Cited in Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/; also BibleHub Illustrator, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/illustrator/jeremiah/45.htm)

J. Oswald Sanders had a similar experience in Auckland, New Zealand, when he was tempted to lobby for a position. The verse arrested him and he let the matter go — and the position later opened to him in God’s timing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)

---

## Traditions: Points of Emphasis and Difference

### Baptist
- **Charles Spurgeon** pressed the application toward Christian workers seeking recognition: “The hen in the farmyard has laid an egg, and feels so proud of the achievement that she must cackle about it… It is so with some professors: their work must be published, or they can do no more.” He added, “If a minister is seeking for souls he will not think of himself.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/illustrator/jeremiah/45.htm)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** connects “seek them not” with Matthew 6:33 and 1 Peter 5:6 — seeking first God’s kingdom and humbling oneself under His hand. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-45.html)
- **Desiring God (Piper’s ministry):** Greg Morse draws the application specifically to men who find their fatigue is actually from selfish ambition, not self-sacrifice. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/secret-pride-makes-a-man-fragile)

### Reformed / Puritan
- **Thomas Manton** (Puritan, on Monergism) treated the text as a reproof of self-love: “Men are mightily addicted to self-love, and when God calleth them to suffer, they think only of their own ease.” The dissuasive “Seek them not” is a call to abandon the dream of a comfortable, trouble-free life. (https://www.monergism.com/do-you-seek-great-things-yourself-seek-them-not-jeremiah-455)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)** emphasises the personal, pastoral application: God still speaks to discouraged servants today. The application section urges believers to “be ambitious only for God’s glory, content that our own names remain unknown if it means we exalt Jesus.” He brings in the stories of Spurgeon and Sanders as testimonies of God’s personal intervention through this verse. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-45/)

### Methodist / Holiness
- **Matthew Henry’s Concise Commentary** (widely used across traditions, but Henry was Presbyterian with broad influence): “Baruch had raised his expectations too high in this world, and that made the distress and trouble he was in harder to be borne. The frowns of the world would not disquiet us, if we did not foolishly flatter ourselves with the hopes of its smiles, and court and covet them.” He adds: “What a folly is it then to seek great things for ourselves here, where every thing is little, and nothing certain!” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/45-5.htm)

### Anglican
- **Ellicott** draws parallels to Elisha rebuking Gehazi’s covetousness (2 Kings 5:26) and Jesus meeting the ambitious request of the sons of Zebedee (Matthew 20:20–23) — a chain of Scripture teaching that self-seeking ambition has no place in the kingdom. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-45.html)

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
- No results were obtained from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the search limits for this chapter. The NET Bible notes and Bible Odyssey would be the sources to consult for text-critical and ANE background perspectives, but could not be retrieved.

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings
- No results were obtained from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits. The deuterocanonical Book of Baruch (bearing his name) testifies to the reverence later generations held for him, and both Jerome (who thought Baruch died in Egypt) and other traditions (that he returned to Babylon after Jeremiah’s death) are noted by Ellicott. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-45.html)

### Debated Popular Teaching
- No prosperity-gospel or word-of-faith commentary sources were located for this chapter. The text itself — with its command *not* to seek great things and its promise of bare survival rather than wealth or success — would stand in marked tension with any teaching that equates faithfulness with earthly prosperity.

---

## Summary of Traditional Interpretation

Jeremiah 45 is a personal word to a faithful but discouraged servant. Baruch, worn down by the dangerous and thankless work of being Jeremiah’s scribe, poured out his complaint to God — a complaint marked by self-focus and disappointed ambition. God’s answer was bracing rather than soothing: “I am about to destroy everything I built — and you are worried about *your* great things? Stop seeking them. In the coming catastrophe, your life alone will be your reward.” Yet this seemingly severe word carried a profound mercy: Baruch’s life *was* preserved through every danger, and the very sufferings he endured for faithfulness gained him an honour across the centuries far greater than anything he could have engineered for himself. The chapter stands as Scripture’s definitive word against self-seeking ambition clothed in religious service, while affirming that God sees, knows, and preserves His own.
